pages.text: Eleven-year-old Adwoa loved the way machines worked. Whenever a bicycle chain slipped or a doorknob rattled in their courtyard, Adwoa reached for her sketchbook and small spanner to study the gears and screws. One Saturday afternoon, while her grandmother’s farm cooperative shelled baskets of dried groundnuts by hand, Adwoa noticed how sore everyone’s thumbs became. Shelling just five kilograms of groundnuts by hand took a whole hour!

One Saturday afternoon, while her grandmother’s farm cooperative shelled baskets of dried groundnuts by hand, Adwoa noticed how sore everyone’s thumbs became.
Shelling just five kilograms of groundnuts by hand took a whole hour!
pages.alt: Eleven-year-old Adwoa sketches in her notebook while watching women and men shell baskets of dried groundnuts by hand.

pages.text: ‘What if I build a pedal-powered groundnut sheller for the school science and craft fair?’ Adwoa said excitedly. Passing by the gate, a neighbour chuckled and shook his head. ‘Adwoa, spanners, gears and welding are for boys! A girl should stick to sweeping and stirring the soup pot, while your brother Kojo learns technical work.’ Adwoa’s smile faded for a moment.

A girl should stick to sweeping and stirring the soup pot, while your brother Kojo learns technical work.’ Adwoa’s smile faded for a moment.
pages.alt: An older neighbour shakes his head dismissively as Adwoa holds her spanner and sketchbook by the courtyard gate.

pages.text: Just then, Papa Kwame stepped out onto the veranda wearing his favourite kitchen apron and holding a wooden ladle, with the rich aroma of kontomire stew floating from the kitchen! Beside him, Mama Esi was reviewing farm-equipment drawings on her tablet, while ten-year-old Kojo hung clean laundry on the line. Papa Kwame smiled warmly at the neighbour and placed a gentle hand on Adwoa’s shoulder.
sentences: Just then, Papa Kwame stepped out onto the veranda wearing his favourite kitchen apron and holding a wooden ladle, with the rich aroma of kontomire stew floating from the kitchen!
Beside him, Mama Esi was reviewing farm-equipment drawings on her tablet, while ten-year-old Kojo hung clean laundry on the line.
Papa Kwame smiled warmly at the neighbour and placed a gentle hand on Adwoa’s shoulder.
pages.alt: Papa Kwame in a kitchen apron holds a ladle beside Mama Esi with her engineering tablet and Kojo hanging laundry.

pages.text: ‘In our home,’ Papa Kwame said kindly, ‘a spanner does not ask whether the hand holding it belongs to a girl or a boy — and neither does a cooking pot! When men and women, boys and girls share caregiving, cooking, budgeting and technical work with mutual respect, every person in the family grows stronger.’ Kojo grinned at his sister. ‘And Adwoa is the best machine builder in our class! Let us build that sheller together!’

‘And Adwoa is the best machine builder in our class!
Let us build that sheller together!’
pages.alt: Papa Kwame, Mama Esi and Kojo encourage Adwoa at the veranda workbench.

pages.text: That afternoon, Mama Esi invited her friend Auntie Serwaa, a qualified Ghanaian mechanical engineer who designed farm machinery, to mentor Adwoa and Kojo. Auntie Serwaa examined Adwoa’s sketch carefully. ‘Your idea uses two simple machines working together,’ Auntie Serwaa explained. ‘The bicycle pedals and chain act as a wheel-and-axle system with a gear ratio, turning a wooden roller inside a curved wire mesh!’
sentences: That afternoon, Mama Esi invited her friend Auntie Serwaa, a qualified Ghanaian mechanical engineer who designed farm machinery, to mentor Adwoa and Kojo.
Auntie Serwaa examined Adwoa’s sketch carefully.
‘Your idea uses two simple machines working together,’ Auntie Serwaa explained.
‘The bicycle pedals and chain act as a wheel-and-axle system with a gear ratio, turning a wooden roller inside a curved wire mesh!’
pages.alt: Mechanical engineer Auntie Serwaa studies Adwoa’s gear-and-roller drawing with Adwoa and Kojo.

pages.text: They gathered clean recycled parts: an old bicycle frame and pedals, a wooden cylinder carved with Papa Kwame’s supervision, and a curved wire screen. In Test 1, when Kojo pedalled fast, the wooden roller sat too close to the wire screen and crushed the groundnut kernels into paste! ‘Do not worry,’ said Auntie Serwaa. ‘Engineers adjust clearances by millimetres until the force is just right.’
sentences: They gathered clean recycled parts: an old bicycle frame and pedals, a wooden cylinder carved with Papa Kwame’s supervision, and a curved wire screen.
In Test 1, when Kojo pedalled fast, the wooden roller sat too close to the wire screen and crushed the groundnut kernels into paste!
‘Do not worry,’ said Auntie Serwaa.
‘Engineers adjust clearances by millimetres until the force is just right.’
pages.alt: Adwoa, Kojo and Auntie Serwaa inspect crushed groundnuts after Test 1 and measure the gap with a ruler.

pages.text: Adwoa measured the average thickness of the groundnut pods and raised the roller bearings by eight millimetres. She also added a small paddle fan driven by a second belt. When the pods cracked open against the screen, the heavy groundnut kernels dropped straight into a clean bowl below, while the gentle wind from the fan blew the light dry shells out through a side chute — winnowing them automatically!
sentences: Adwoa measured the average thickness of the groundnut pods and raised the roller bearings by eight millimetres.

pages.alt: Adwoa adjusts the roller height with her spanner and adds a small belt-driven fan to blow away the light shells.

pages.text: Now it was time to measure the machine’s performance using maths! By hand, one person shelled five kilograms of groundnuts in one hour. When Adwoa and Kojo took turns pedalling their adjusted machine for ten minutes, it cleanly shelled five kilograms! ‘Ten minutes is one-sixth of an hour,’ calculated Adwoa. ‘Five kilograms times six equals thirty kilograms per hour — six times faster than shelling by hand!’

pages.alt: Kojo times ten minutes on a stopwatch while Adwoa weighs five kilograms of cleanly shelled groundnuts on a scale.

pages.text: At the district STEM and Agricultural Fair on Friday, students, teachers and local farmers gathered around Adwoa and Kojo’s booth. Adwoa explained the gear ratio between the large front chainring and the smaller rear sprocket, while Kojo demonstrated how easily the pedals turned and how the fan separated shells from kernels without crushing the nuts.

pages.alt: At the district STEM fair, Adwoa explains the gear mechanism while Kojo pedals and farmers watch clean groundnuts pour into the bowl.

pages.text: The very neighbour who had doubted Adwoa on Saturday stepped forward, examined the clean unbroken groundnut kernels in the bowl, and smiled sheepishly. ‘Adwoa, I was wrong,’ he said respectfully in front of the crowd. ‘Your mind and your hands have built something that will save our women and men hours of painful work every harvest. May our cooperative order two machines from your workshop?’

pages.alt: The neighbour shakes Adwoa’s hand respectfully at the science fair while Papa Kwame, Mama Esi and Auntie Serwaa beam.

pages.text: That evening, after Papa Kwame and Kojo washed the supper dishes and Mama Esi and Adwoa sketched improvements for a maize-shelling attachment, Adwoa wrote on the first page of her engineering notebook: Talent has no gender, and teamwork has no limits. When every girl and every boy is free to learn, build and care, the whole community rises together.

activities.question: How did Papa Kwame and Mama Esi respond to the idea that technical work is only for boys and housework is only for girls?
options: They showed that boys and girls can both build machines and share home duties
They locked away Adwoa’s spanner and sketchbook
They told Kojo he was never allowed to enter the kitchen
activities.explanation: Papa Kwame and Mama Esi modelled shared caregiving and domestic work while encouraging both Adwoa and Kojo in engineering.

activities.definition: Using a current of air to blow away light chaff or shells from heavier grain or kernels
distractors: Boiling groundnuts in a pot of salted water
Painting a bicycle frame purple and gold

activities.question: When Test 1 crushed the groundnuts into paste, how did Adwoa fix the machine?
options: She measured the pods and raised the roller clearance by 8 millimetres
She removed the pedals and threw the machine away
She painted the wooden roller a brighter colour
activities.explanation: By measuring the pod size and increasing the gap between the roller and the wire mesh by 8 mm, the shells cracked without crushing the kernels.

activities.question: If Adwoa’s machine shells 5 kg in 10 minutes, how many kilograms does it shell in 1 hour (60 minutes)?
options: 30 kg per hour — six times faster than 5 kg per hour by hand
activities.explanation: There are six 10-minute periods in 60 minutes, so 5 kg × 6 = 30 kg per hour.

activities.prompt: Order the steps of how Adwoa and her family built the groundnut sheller.
items: Spot the painful hand-shelling problem and sketch a pedal-powered design.
Test the prototype, adjust the roller gap by 8 mm, and add a winnowing fan.
Demonstrate the 30-kg-per-hour machine at the district STEM fair.
